Messages.Author: Alex Broadhead
Messages.Body:
Howdy,

Before you say, "Argh, not another play to win thread!" and tune out -
I'm not really intending this to dredge up any of the other threads'
content. Where the concerns of those threads has been more or less
entirely a series of hypotheticals, I'm hoping that this thread can
bring us back to actual practice.

In the spirit of Ira's request for 'case studies' as teaching aids for
judges, and in the spirit of Derek's and my suspicion that actual
actionable abuses of 'Play to Win' are few and far between and
unsubtle when they occur, I wonder if judges who have actually
enforced 'Play to Win' could post suitably anonymized transcriptions
of their enforcement actions. No names, please, but it'd be nice to
have a) the game state at the point of the ruling, in as much detail
as is useful, b) the ruling, c) the thought process leading to the
ruling and d) the effects of the ruling.

Note that I'm mostly looking for cases where the ruling was that the
player in question _wasn't_ Playing to Win and needed to somehow alter
their play. Interesting cases where a ruling was called for and it
was decided that the player was, in fact, conforming would probably be
useful as well, and I can even supply one of those myself. (It was a
while ago, so my memory is fuzzy, and I was not the judge.)

Finals of a small tourney. Table was me (!Ventrue bleed) -> Samedi
S&B -> Brujah A (vote/bleed) -> Brujah B (Euro/titled bruise) ->
Brujah C (bruise); the combination of Samedi stealth bleed and Brujah
B back-rush has already erased Brujah A. Brujah C is on the ropes
with three vamps and something like 1-3 pool remaining - and he
apparently has neither bleed nor rush in his deck, just combat.
Brujah B is in decent shape, with minions along the lines of Pascek,
Theo, and/or Donal and ten-ish pool. The Samedi have 2-3 minions up
and Laptopped, and are in decent shape with the +6 pool, though they
are generally vulnerable to my bleed. I am running low on pool (<10)
- I haven't been foolish enough to block the Brujah, and so am
steadily losing 2-3 pool per turn. I have something like Neally and
Tanner and Stoddard out, and they are getting low on blood.

Brujah B, on his turn, decides that the appropriate course is not for
him to attempt to bleed out Brujah C (who has one untapped minion),
but rather to cut a deal to split the table with him. He offers to
erase my minions so that Brujah C can move forward more rapidly, take
me and the Samedi out, and then concede the last two VP to him (Brujah
B), making the table a 2/2/1 split. I find this plan objectionable,
as it seems to me to be conceding a 'reasonable' chance at a 4 VP win.
Further extenuating circumstances: Brujah B has spent significant
effort every game that I have played with him attacking me no matter
where I sit relative to him; Brujah B and Brujah C play in the same
gaming group, which interacts only rarely with the local group. I
call the judge.

The judge argues, in essence, that Play to Win is unenforceable, so
his ruling is not particularly germane. What is germane is the fact
that I have left out, and which I had not considered: Brujah B was
seeded first. Thus, he was still playing to win, as a 2/2 tie would
break in his favor.

Of course, Brujah B's own justifications were nowhere near that clear:
he argued that he would lose too many minions trying to bleed out
Brujah C to be effective against me. Given that he'd previously shown
Deflection and seat-changing votes, and had a stealth bleed predator,
and had chosen to sit as predator to Brujah C, this line of argument
struck me as hysterical.

Once the tiebreak had been pointed out, there was no longer any
substance to my argument that Brujah B was giving away VP, and so play
resumed with the deal in force. Brujah B Famed some one of my
minions. I top-decked a few more Skin of Steel to go with the Rolling
with the Punches already in my hand and fought Brujah B to a
standstill. Brujah C was still going to need several Turns to bleed
me out. The Samedi quietly bled the hell out of Brujah B (though I
think it took two Turns), and then Brujah C. I conceded that I didn't
have the bleed to go through the extra 12 pool before the Samedi took
me out. Entirely predictable, really. (And one of the few cases I've
seen where 'salmoning' might have actually worked.)

Anyway, Brujah B was clearly not playing particularly well, but he was
minimally playing to win, at least in terms of his argument (and
probably in his mind as well). I think I would have to rule against
myself.

Other examples?

Thanks,
Alex

Messages.Author: Ira
Messages.Body:
Hey Alex,

In my opinion, this is a great case study topic because it comes up
very infrequently, but when it does, the judge's ruling is extremely
significant. These are the perfect things to practice and explore in
a case study - low likelihood, high consequence rulings.

First, and most importantly, finalists are assumed to be playing to
win. That is, whatever they do (even if it's ousting themselves from
the beginning), they are considered to be playing to win. I use the
word "assume" above in the mathematical proof sort of meaning - it is
simply true.

LSJ has patiently elaborated on this in a previous thread. The
following post is the most relevant, but I found the whole thread to
be enlightening:

http://tinyurl.com/49gu5

So, I'll change the case study to a preliminary round and respond
with my thoughts accordingly.

> Finals of a small tourney.

Remember, play to win doesn't really effect the finals, since
finalists are always playing to win no matter what they do. This took
me a little while to comprehend and internalize, and it's significant.

In a prelim round, I would take Brujah B to the side, and find out
his true intentions and thoughts. Maybe he was planning on some seat
switching votes, or breaking his word, or something like that. Maybe
he was just offering the deal to throw off Brujah C. If Brujah B
claimed to me that he would consider breaking his word if Brujah C
looked weak, or might call a seat switching vote, it would be
extremely difficult for me to claim that he wasn't playing to win. I
would surely let him play as he wished in that case. Note: the player
could lie to the judge about his intentions, and there's not much the
judge can do about that. In that regard, if players are willing to
lie to judges, the play to win rule becomes much less enforceable.

In the case of Brujah C, I would also have to be convinced that
Brujah C has no reasonable chance to win, because Brujah C is also
giving up the GW by making this deal. I'd have a similar conversation
with Brujah C, and see what his intentions were.

Perhaps Brujah B would say to me that he truly wanted to honor the
deal, and wouldn't seat switch. In that case, I'd only let him make
the deal if he claimed that he really didn't have a reasonable (5%)
chance of getting a GW, and I was convinced of that. From the limited
information available, I probably wouldn't let him make such a deal.
I figure he probably has at least 5% chance of getting a GW from the
situation you described. I would let the player discuss this point
with me and explain why he had no hope, and perhaps I would be
pursuaded.

Then again, perhaps I'm thinking about this wrong - perhaps their
intentions for keeping or not keeping the deal don't matter. Does
that matter? I'm not sure. I think I have to assume their intentions
are to keep the deal, and in that case, is the deal legal to make?
It's only legal to make a deal like that if both of them no longer
have a reasonable chance at a GW. If either one had a reasonable
chance at a GW, I should prevent them from making the deal.

Regardless, even if I disallowed the table splitting deal at that
time, I almost certainly wouldn't mandate any specific plays. I
wouldn't force him to bleed or do anything. With the Fame, I might
ask him to clarify how putting Fame on your vampire was helping him
play to win without a deal in place. I would ask for such a
clarification in private, and I'd probably add time to the clock if it
took longer than 2 minutes for all this discussion.

As a judge, I am *extremely* reluctant to dictate specific plays, or
even prohibit specific plays. I'm slightly more willing to prohibit
deals if they obviously go against play to win.

> The Samedi quietly bled the hell out of Brujah B (though I
> think it took two Turns), and then Brujah C.

If Brujah B was playing Euro Brujah, then perhaps it was his plan to
bounce bleeds.

> Other examples?

I have a decent one, but I'll post it separately in this thread when
I have more time.

Ira

German Qualifier, 2nd round.

3 players left, plenty of time.
Player A has 1 VP and plays obf-pre with AUS-bounce, not to be ousted
soon.
Player B has no VP's, !malk stealthbleed with AUS-bounce, not to be
ousted soon.
Player C (me) has 1 VP, Qadir-bloat-n-AR, 2 ARs in play, not in that
good health, but will survive at least some turns, in hope to finally
draw his miniontaps.

I would say chances to win were about 40-40-20

Player A proposes a deal that would give B a VP, and A the table. B
agrees. I call the judge. the Judge agrees that B's chances are above
reasonable and forbids the deal.
Player A then proposes a 2-2-1 deal with player B, the judge forbids
this for the same reasons.
player A then proposes to help B oust me and then fight it out. I nor
the judge can think of a reason why he shouldn't. and so it happens.

B wins the game (by topdecking a wake)

I think the judge made the right decisions in this case.

W

> the beginning), they are considered to be playing to win. I use the
> word "assume" above in the mathematical proof sort of meaning - it is
> simply true.

This is going to be kind of a tangent from the case study topic, but I
don't think I agree with this. In my opinion, finalists are by no means
exempt from the "Unsportsmanlike Conduct" part of the tournament rules
that says "Players must not play toward goals that conflict with the
goal of the game as stated in the V:TES rulebook (e.g., attacking
certain players on the basis of their V:EKN ratings or overall
tournament standing, etc.)."

Yes, finalists will normally be playing to win (or maximize their final
standing) because there is no advantage to doing otherwise. But that
doesn't mean they can do otherwise for spite's sake, or on the basis of
other player's VEKN ratings, etc, just because they're in the finals.
They still may not collude or bribe each other.

My reading of Scott's posts on this topic is that finalists are assumed
to be playing to win because they normally shouldn't have any reason to
do otherwise. If they *are* doing otherwise, their possible motives
should still be examined, because there *are* rules against throwing
games, even in the finals.

Josh

> In my opinion, finalists are by no means exempt from the

I agree that finalists must still behave in a sportmanlike way.

> They still may not collude or bribe each other.

Agreed.

> My reading of Scott's posts on this topic is that finalists are assumed
> to be playing to win because they normally shouldn't have any reason to
> do otherwise. If they *are* doing otherwise, their possible motives
> should still be examined, because there *are* rules against throwing
> games, even in the finals.

What about ousting yourself? LSJ said pretty explicitly that it
shouldn't be prevented assuming no other violations like collusion,
etc. Specifically this post:

http://groups.google.com/groups?hl=en&lr=&ie=UTF-8&selm=HRgkc.4291%24Xj6.68503%40bgtnsc04-news.ops.worldnet.att.net

and the response "Pathological, but no." That whole post shows how a
greater degree of play-to-win freedom is given to finalists that's not
given to players in a preliminary round.

Here's another example:
I'm in 5th place in the tournament, and the final round is about to
start. I need to leave in 10 minutes. If I don't sit down at the
final table, the best I can do is 6th place (at least, I think that's
the way it works now.) The current V:EKN rating system also
encourages being at the final table.

So, I sit down, and then I immediately oust myself. I'm not colluding
with anyone, but I'm also not actively trying to win. Should the
judge prohibit this behavior? In a preliminary round, absolutely. In
a final round, I previously believed that the judge should prohibit
it, but LSJ's post above states clearly (to me at least) that the
judge should NOT prohibit it.

Also, I'm unclear whether or not the player, knowing he must leave in
10 minutes, is engaging in unsportsmanlike conduct. For a preliminary
round, yes. For a final round, I think not, since that player is
basically allowed to play however he wants, whatever "gives you the
best bang for your buck in terms of winning." [LSJ, in the post
referenced above.]

Finally, as a judge, I would double check that the player didn't tell
anyone else that he had to leave, because otherwise it could be
collusion.

Then again, maybe in that case it would be better to have a 4 player
final, and still have the 5th place person place 5th?

Also, does it change the situation any if the player's time limit is
30 minutes, or 60 minutes, or 110 minutes?

Ira

Messages.Author: Ira
Messages.Body:
Here is another example from a Final. I'm not sure if the ruling
should be different for a final or not, given Joshua's good points
about unsportsmanship conduct rules still applying (perhaps.)

Meth A (1st Seed) !Toreador weenie/embrace vote w/ Foundation Exhibit
Meth B (3rd Seed) Tzim intercept combat
Meth C (5th Seed) !Malk/Malk stealth bleed w/ fortitiude
Meth D (4th seed) Ahrimanes toolbox vote
Meth E (2nd seed) 2nd tradition/animalism block long range combat

The game was very slow overall. Meth D was getting pretty frustrated
because the one turn he tapped out, Meth C bled for a lot and would
otherwise do nothing. Meth E would block everything that Meth D did.
Meth A couldn't take any actions safely because otherwise he'd be
blocked (Maris Strek was controlled by Meth E.) Meth B bled for 1 a
bunch and Meth C never blocked.

With about 20-25 minutes left, Meth C offers to do nothing to Meth D
for several turns (I think 3) so that Meth D could tap out "safely"
and would have the chance oust Meth E. In return, Meth D would oust
himself if his own oust attempt failed. I think the turn limits were
nebulous and not specific, but both Meths seemed to be OK with that
and willing to keep the deal. Meth D makes a valiant attempt for a
couple of turns, but Meth E apparently has an endless supply of untaps
and 2nd traditions.

Meth A, who is seeded first, really just wants the game to go to time.
He tries to convince Meth D not to transfer out, because on his turn,
he could call votes that hurt Meth E. Meth D sticks around for
another turn. Meth A doesn't call any votes on his turn. There is
about 1 minute left.

Meth B plays revelations at basic, discards a Confusion from Meth C's
hand. Maybe bleeds for 1. Ends his turn.

Meth C bleeds for 2, putting Meth D at 4 pool, and ends his turn.

About 30 seconds left.

Meth D wants to oust himself, and transfers out. Objection from Meth
A. Judge is called over with 13 seconds left on the clock, and time
is stopped.

Judge rules that Meth D is allowed to transfer out because he's
following a legally made deal, and also because it's the final.

Time resumes, Meth A is understandably upset, and tells Meth E, who
has been diligently trying to kill Meth A the whole game, that he'll
oust himself on his turn. Meth E, with three untapped minions to Meth
A's 3 pool, bleeds for one and ousts Meth A just before the buzzer.

Meth A had an untapped minion, and a telepathic misdirection in hand.

The Judge rules that Meth A could allow himself to be ousted because
it was the finals, even though he was obviously not playing to win.
Had Meth A stayed alive, he would have placed 2nd. By allowing
himself to be ousted, he placed 4th.

I'm not sure where to draw the line between poor play (i.e. not
blocking or bouncing) and willingly getting ousted. I think in a
prelim round, I wouldn't have allowed Meth A to let himself be killed
as he did.

In the finals, I think that I would rule just as the Judge ruled, and
that is Meth A is allowed to do what he wants. From observation, I
believe the primary motivation from Meth A was an emotional reaction
to having the tournament win stolen away from him, and he wanted to
regain some control over the situation, even if that meant giving the
win to someone else. He didn't care at all about the difference
between 2nd or 4th; it was all-or-nothing. As a note, the prize
structure was also that way - 1st place got 20 boosters, everyone else
got nothing.

Furthermore, I'm not sure if there's a difference in this case between
transferring oneself out, and allowing oneself to get bled out. There
is a slight difference, but not much. My rulings as a judge in the
case wouldn't have been any different.

It's not like Meth A made a calculated decision to spite Meth E by
preventing him from cycling stealth or a Contingency Planning; Meth A
actively wanted to die, and could have lived at least one more round
if he desired.

Ira

Hey Kevin,

> If I was judging at that final table where you ousted yourself because you
> had to leave in X minutes and then tried to claim 5th place in the
> tournament + prize support, I'd put you down as the 5th place finalist,
> give your prize support to the person in 6th place, and report you to WW
> as a "Disqualification without prize for severe Unsportsmanlike conduct"
> [VEKN JG 20]. You could have it out with LSJ and Robert Goudie from
> there.

If this happened in a prelim round, I'd agree with a severe penalty.

But we're talking about the final round, for which the 5th place
player has already earned his spot. LSJ previously said that no
finalist would oust himself from the beginning of the game:

http://groups.google.com/groups?q=g:thl3473466833d&dq=&hl=en&lr=&ie=UTF-8&selm=rnpkc.7258%24Xj6.114601%40bgtnsc04-news.ops.worldnet.att.net

This seems to me to be a case where the finalist really does want to
oust himself, but isn't breaking any rule other than play-to-win. And
since finalists are ASSUMED to be playing-to-win, it's impossible for
that finalist (who is ousting himself) to not be playing-to-win.

Does anyone else have thoughts on this?

LSJ, given this situation of a finalist wanting to oust himself,
would you prohibit it under the sportsmanship rules, or would you
allow it to happen because the finalist is assumed to be playing to
win?

> I'd love to hear how outsing yourself gives you the best bang
> for your buck in terms of winning. ;)

If I play and oust myself, I come in 5th and I get a better rating.
If I don't play at all, I come in 6th and get a worse rating. 5th is
better than 6th.

Note: I could be wrong about the rankings of a finalist who opts not
to play in the final, but I'm pretty sure the 6th seeded person will
place higher than the 5th seeded person after the tournament is over.

Ira

ever allow him to let himself be ousted like that. If things go wrong
for me, should I be allowed to behave like that, just because I'm in
the finals?

I would like to know what you folks think about this, but for me it
feels so wrong.

(snip)

> From observation, I
> believe the primary motivation from Meth A was an emotional reaction
> to having the tournament win stolen away from him, and he wanted to
> regain some control over the situation, even if that meant giving the
> win to someone else.

That's my point... That's an emotional reaction, and because of that
reaction he fell into unsportmanlike behavior, in my opinion...

> He didn't care at all about the difference
> between 2nd or 4th; it was all-or-nothing. As a note, the prize
> structure was also that way - 1st place got 20 boosters, everyone else
> got nothing.

As a judge, I don't think 2nd is the same as 4th. I feel like
enforcing the players to rank as high as possible, even 1st is not
possible anymore. And I regard the prize as an off-game issue, so it
should not influence players' in-game decisions.

Thanks for the debate. I hope I could express myself well here,
whithout sounding too harsh.. =)

Cheers,

Luiz

Messages.Author: Alex Broadhead
Messages.Body:
Howdy Ira,

> Here is another example from a Final. I'm not sure if the ruling
> should be different for a final or not, given Joshua's good points
> about unsportsmanship conduct rules still applying (perhaps.)
>
> Meth A (1st Seed) !Toreador weenie/embrace vote w/ Foundation Exhibit
> Meth B (3rd Seed) Tzim intercept combat
> Meth C (5th Seed) !Malk/Malk stealth bleed w/ fortitiude
> Meth D (4th seed) Ahrimanes toolbox vote
> Meth E (2nd seed) 2nd tradition/animalism block long range combat

Why on earth did Meth A choose to sit there? Between two interceptors
seems like a really bad choice for him. I'm guessing he didn't know
what he was getting into? Not that it's relevant to the rulings.

> The game was very slow overall.

With every player most likely fielding some intercept (except maybe
the Malks), and at least two serious intercept combat decks, this
hardly seems surprising. Sounds like several players could benefit
from reading Derek's writings on winning with intercept...



I agree. The deal was either legal or not at the time it was made.
No one objected then - it's too late now. Honoring a legal deal is
legal. And that Meth A is calling a judge after not upholding his end
of the other deal takes serious chutzpah.

> Time resumes, Meth A is understandably upset, and tells Meth E, who
> has been diligently trying to kill Meth A the whole game, that he'll
> oust himself on his turn. Meth E, with three untapped minions to Meth
> A's 3 pool, bleeds for one and ousts Meth A just before the buzzer.
>
> Meth A had an untapped minion, and a telepathic misdirection in hand.
>
> The Judge rules that Meth A could allow himself to be ousted because
> it was the finals, even though he was obviously not playing to win.
> Had Meth A stayed alive, he would have placed 2nd. By allowing
> himself to be ousted, he placed 4th.

I guess C called the judge? He's the only one (other than A) who
suffers by A's play:

Before: C (1), A (2), E (3), B (4), D (5)
After: E (1), C (2), B (3), A (4), D (5)

Meth C certainly has a case. Meth A will earn a half-point more and a
higher final placement by defending himself, unless something wacky
happens. He cannot argue that his position is lost. I don't see how
his play is 'sportsmanlike' either. Spite is more or less the
opposite of sportsmanlike.

Now if A had time to make a deal to split the winnings with E for
self-ousting, I guess that'd be legal, though it'd still suck IMO...

> I'm not sure where to draw the line between poor play (i.e. not
> blocking or bouncing) and willingly getting ousted. I think in a
> prelim round, I wouldn't have allowed Meth A to let himself be killed
> as he did.

A has already shown serious chutzpah, but I guess I don't see him
having the cojones to sit there and tell a judge that he just couldn't
play any better... Especially not after making the final. This is
where the 'unsubtle' bit factors in. Meth A can try to grey the issue
all he wants, but I just don't see any competent judge buying an
incompetence defense here.

> In the finals, I think that I would rule just as the Judge ruled, and
> that is Meth A is allowed to do what he wants. From observation, I
> believe the primary motivation from Meth A was an emotional reaction
> to having the tournament win stolen away from him, and he wanted to
> regain some control over the situation, even if that meant giving the
> win to someone else.

This sounds like an astute analysis of the psychology. But 'playing
to exercise control over the outcome' is not the same as 'playing to
win'. In fact, it's the opposite in this case.

I don't really understand the 'presumed playing to win' theory you
have extracted from LSJs posts on the subject, though I can see where
it comes from. Perhaps, though, LSJ just meant to point out the
difference between prelims, where one could possibly play 'to the
final' rather than 'to win', and the final, where you can't play 'to
the final' anymore? Otherwise, I don't know how to reconcile
intentional losing play with a presumption that everyone is playing to
win.

> He didn't care at all about the difference
> between 2nd or 4th; it was all-or-nothing. As a note, the prize
> structure was also that way - 1st place got 20 boosters, everyone else
> got nothing.

Yuck. I guess there were still ratings, but many players don't care
about them. The interaction between this prize structure and 'play to
win' is not good. In prelims you play for the GW, then VP, then
nothing. Here, in a practical sense, you play for the GW, then
nothing; VPs short of a GW are meaningless, and eliding 'no GW' with
'lost position' becomes reasonable. I can see how this would cause
mutations of 'play to win'. It might be worth rethinking the prize
structure in the future.

Thanks for the example(s),
Alex

Messages.Author: Ira
Messages.Body:
Hey Alex,

> Why on earth did Meth A choose to sit there? Between two interceptors
> seems like a really bad choice for him. I'm guessing he didn't know
> what he was getting into?

Right.

> Sounds like several players could benefit
> from reading Derek's writings on winning with intercept...

There were excellent players sitting at that table. All them made it
to the finals, so clearly they were doing something right.

> No one objected then - it's too late now.

I disagree. It's not too late to object, though objecting when it
was originally made would be better. But a Judge can always be called
over, and I wouldn't automatically dismiss the claim "because it's too
late."

> And that Meth A is calling a judge after not upholding his end
> of the other deal takes serious chutzpah.

We can make the case study whatever we want, but just for clarity on
what actually happened, Meth A never promised that he'd do anything,
he just presented some possibilities, and some logic why Meth D
shouldn't oust himself.

> I guess C called the judge?

The judge was called over when Meth D wanted to oust himself. In the
ensuing discussion, Meth A clarified that he could also oust himself
if he wanted. It all came up at once.

> I don't really understand the 'presumed playing to win' theory you
> have extracted from LSJs posts on the subject

Really? I thought LSJ was explicit. I provided the base-case of not
playing to win (i.e. ousting oneself from the outset), and LSJ said
that a judge shouldn't stop it. I provided the URL earlier, and I'll
link it again because that's easier than trying to paraphrase:

http://groups.google.com/groups?q=author:LSJ+pathological+group:rec.games.trading-cards.jyhad&hl=en&lr=&ie=UTF-8&group=rec.games.trading-cards.jyhad&selm=HRgkc.4291%24Xj6.68503%40bgtnsc04-news.ops.worldnet.att.net&rnum=1

Then again, LSJ's recent response in this thread seems to contradict
it. I'm sure it doesn't actually contradict, I just don't understand
why not.

I'm going to give up for a while, because honestly I'm totally
confused about what LSJ really wants us to do. It seems to me that it
should be simple, but I feel like I can't get a straight answer;
conversely, I wouldn't be at all surprised if LSJ feels like he's
given a straight answer 10 times in a row, and I'm just an idiot for
not getting it.

LSJ, it's frustrating that you're unwilling to give case studies,
because I so strongly believe that it's the best way to learn good
decision making for grey areas. For instance, you could state how you
would rule in the several cases presented in this thread. That would
be more enlightening to me than your recent, correct, precise, and
concise statements. I know you work really hard for us, and I
appreciate it deeply. I just wish you'd give the case studies a try,
because it'd be a really good time-to-benefit ratio for you and for
us.

Ira, who is tired

I appear to be resurrecting a thread that everyone else has decided to

"Ira" <ira...@yahoo.com> wrote in message
news:500e74e.04072...@posting.google.com...

[Alex Broadhead wrote]

> > No one objected then - it's too late now.
>
> I disagree. It's not too late to object, though objecting when it
> was originally made would be better. But a Judge can always be called
> over, and I wouldn't automatically dismiss the claim "because it's too
> late."

Yes, I would agree with you on that, Ira. And on the case-study
question regarding D wanting to uphold his deal and self-oust, I would
also probably say that D *can* uphold the bargain and self-oust just
before time if he wants to, although in my personal opinion he is
harming his own position by doing so and would be better off not
self-ousting. :-)

I could go on to claim that Meth D has put himself into the position of
being nothing but a tool for Meth C, and is now (presumably
unintentionally) playing to lose. But it sounds like Meth D would claim
that he has no reasonable chance to win (or earn any more VPs) without
making the deal with C. Again I might disagree; if you can be patient
and stick around longer, you almost always have *some* reasonable chance
of improving your position. But I would probably prefer not to make D
play the way I would play, instead of the way he would play, as a judge.

> > I don't really understand the 'presumed playing to win' theory you
> > have extracted from LSJs posts on the subject
>
> Really? I thought LSJ was explicit. I provided the base-case of not
> playing to win (i.e. ousting oneself from the outset), and LSJ said
> that a judge shouldn't stop it. I provided the URL earlier, and I'll
> link it again because that's easier than trying to paraphrase:

Here's a shorter link to that thread:

http://tinylink.com/?3M751ZKrgy

My interpretation of LSJ's answers there is not that finalists can do
whatever they want. It's that they are assumed to be playing to win in
the absence of evidence to the contrary, since they should have no
incentive to do otherwise. That's why it's "pathological" for a
finalist to oust himself as soon as he sits down. I'm not sure why he
went on to say "but no" after using the word pathological, but in that
last post in the thread, he wrote "Because he wouldn't do it, that's
why. It's a faulty premise. It needs no special regulating." To me,
that means that the immediate self-oust is not explicitly prohibited
only because it should never happen: there should normally be no reason
for a finalist to oust himself as soon as he sits down, because he
cannot benefit from doing so. If there *is* some out-of-game
consideration that is leading him to do such a thing, he *can* be
violating the sportsmanship rules, and that *can* be corrected by the
judge.

That's my interpretation, at least.

> LSJ, it's frustrating that you're unwilling to give case studies,
> because I so strongly believe that it's the best way to learn good
> decision making for grey areas. For instance, you could state how you
> would rule in the several cases presented in this thread. That would
> be more enlightening to me than your recent, correct, precise, and
> concise statements. I know you work really hard for us, and I
> appreciate it deeply. I just wish you'd give the case studies a try,
> because it'd be a really good time-to-benefit ratio for you and for
> us.

I agree that this would be useful to us judges. I think he's not
willing to do it because he feels that no newsgroup-post case study can
sufficiently specify everything about a game, in the level of detail
that would be available to an actual judge "on the ground". But I have
to agree with you that if the level of detail that can be put down in
words is sufficient for lawyers, it ought to be sufficient for us too.
:-)

Josh

Messages.Author: Joshua Duffin
Messages.Body:
"Ira" <ira...@yahoo.com> wrote in message
news:500e74e.04072...@posting.google.com...

hi again Ira,

> Here's another example:
> I'm in 5th place in the tournament, and the final round is about to
> start. I need to leave in 10 minutes. If I don't sit down at the
> final table, the best I can do is 6th place (at least, I think that's
> the way it works now.) The current V:EKN rating system also
> encourages being at the final table.

> Also, I'm unclear whether or not the player, knowing he must leave in

> 10 minutes, is engaging in unsportsmanlike conduct. For a preliminary
> round, yes. For a final round, I think not, since that player is
> basically allowed to play however he wants, whatever "gives you the
> best bang for your buck in terms of winning." [LSJ, in the post
> referenced above.]

I think this is unsportsmanlike, yes. Whatever gives you the best bang
for the buck in terms of winning is still subject to being a good sport,
and sitting down for a final that you can only play ten minutes of is
not fair (IMO) to the other players.

> Then again, maybe in that case it would be better to have a 4 player
> final, and still have the 5th place person place 5th?

Hmm. I wouldn't be inclined to go this route. I would probably prefer
to drop the "has to leave in 10 minutes" player from the finals (he
might place 6th for the ratings system, I'm not sure if what happens in
these cases is well-defined).

> Also, does it change the situation any if the player's time limit is
> 30 minutes, or 60 minutes, or 110 minutes?

Good question. I think that in principle, it does not: if a player
knows ahead of time that he cannot participate in the full potential
length of the final game, he should not sit down for just part of it.
On the other hand, I would be somewhat sympathetic to the 110-minute
time limit, in that there is a somewhat reasonable chance that the game
could be over (or at least over for that particular player) by that
time. Still, I think it's probably best for players not to sit down for
the finals if they wouldn't be able to play the whole thing.

(Hopefully I've addressed the other part of your post in my other post
to this thread - it didn't seem like there was anything more for me to
say about the general "play to win" case in response to this post.)

Josh

always believes in the heart of the cards
